meta.description: Not Thomas Edison. The line comes from naturalist John Burroughs in The Atlantic Monthly (October 1921); Wikiquote lists it among lines misattributed to Edison.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I am much less interested in what is called God's word than in God's deeds'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Thomas Edison. It's John Burroughs, in The Atlantic Monthly (October 1921) — Wikiquote files it under lines misattributed to Edison.

answer.label: Not Thomas Edison — actually John Burroughs
answer.sourceLine: The documented source is not Edison but the naturalist John Burroughs, in his posthumously published correspondence “Religious Contrasts: Letters of a Pantheist and a Churchman,” in The Atlantic Monthly, Vol. 128, No. 4 (October 1921), p. 520 — where Wikiquote lists it among lines misattributed to Edison. Burroughs and Edison were camping companions, which likely explains how the pantheist’s words drifted onto the more famous inventor.

source.excerpt: I am much less interested in what is called God’s word than in God’s deeds. All bibles are man-made.
trail: Wikiquote’s Thomas Edison page places this line in its Misattributed section, not among his sourced quotations.

It credits the wording to John Burroughs, in “Religious Contrasts: Letters of a Pantheist and a Churchman,” The Atlantic Monthly (October 1921), p. 520 — a citation independently repeated by quote aggregators that flag it “Misattributed.”
That October 1921 volume of the magazine survives in full at HathiTrust; Burroughs had died in March 1921, so the piece ran posthumously.
No Edison speech, interview, letter, or diary is offered by any source as the origin of this exact wording.
source.excerptNote: The two sentences travel together; the second, “All bibles are man-made,” is likewise carried by Wikiquote in the same misattributed entry.

sourceLink.text: The Atlantic Monthly, Vol. 128 (July–December 1921) at HathiTrust

source.rightsNote: The line was first published in The Atlantic Monthly in October 1921 — well before the 1930 U.S. copyright cutoff — so the text is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: John Burroughs
author.heading: John Burroughs
author.bio: John Burroughs (1837–1921) was one of America’s most widely read nature essayists, a founding figure of literary nature writing whose books blended close observation with a frankly pantheist philosophy that leaned toward religious skepticism. He was also a celebrated companion of the industrial age: he took long camping trips with Thomas Edison, Henry Ford, and Harvey Firestone — the group the press dubbed the “Vagabonds” — which is very likely how one of his lines came to be pinned on Edison.

misattribution.heading: Why it lands on Edison
misattribution.intro: Thomas Edison is one of the internet’s great magnets for freethinking one-liners, and this is one that isn’t his. The words belong to his friend and camping companion John Burroughs.

items.why: Quote pages, image memes, and aggregators routinely stamp this on Edison, but Wikiquote files it under Misattributed and offers no Edison source for it.

The sentence appears in Burroughs’s “Religious Contrasts: Letters of a Pantheist and a Churchman,” in The Atlantic Monthly, Vol. 128 (October 1921), p. 520 — the pantheist voice in that correspondence is Burroughs’s own.

misattribution.truthLine: The pantheist idiom is pure Burroughs; the fame is Edison’s — and the two men camped together as the “Vagabonds,” which is almost certainly how the line changed hands.

context.heading: Two skeptics, one line
lead: Edison did hold irreverent views about scripture — he gave interviews doubting a personal God and a literal soul — so a line like this sounds like him, which is exactly why it sticks. But sounding like someone is not the same as being said by them.

The actual author, John Burroughs, wrote from a self-described pantheist standpoint: reverence directed at nature and “God’s deeds” rather than at any book. Published months after his death in 1921, the passage is a tidy statement of that creed — and a reminder of how easily a famous friend’s name can swallow a quieter writer’s words.
context.pull: The pantheist voice is Burroughs’s; the byline the internet gave it is Edison’s.
